crisis_types.definition: Organized violence between state or non-state armed groups resulting in displacement, civilian casualties, and disruption of essential services.
crisis_types.affected_populations: Internally displaced persons (IDPs), refugees, host communities, conflict-affected civilians

crisis_types.definition: Sudden shaking of the ground caused by tectonic plate movement, capable of destroying buildings and infrastructure within seconds.
crisis_types.affected_populations: Urban populations in seismically active zones, people in non-engineered structures

crisis_types.definition: Overflow of water onto normally dry land, including riverine, coastal, and flash floods. The most common natural disaster globally.
crisis_types.affected_populations: Floodplain communities, low-lying coastal populations, informal settlement residents

crisis_types.definition: Extended period of deficient rainfall relative to normal conditions, leading to water scarcity, crop failure, and potential famine.
crisis_types.affected_populations: Pastoralist communities, rain-fed agriculture populations, children under 5

crisis_types.definition: Rotating storm system with sustained winds exceeding 119 km/h, causing destruction through wind, storm surge, and flooding.
crisis_types.affected_populations: Coastal communities, island nations, populations in informal settlements

crisis_types.definition: Rapid spread of infectious disease affecting a large number of people, overwhelming health systems and disrupting society.
crisis_types.affected_populations: Overcrowded settings (camps, urban slums), immunocompromised, healthcare workers

crisis_types.definition: Extreme food crisis where at least 20% of households face extreme food gaps, acute malnutrition exceeds 30%, and death rate exceeds 2 per 10,000 per day (IPC Phase 5).
crisis_types.affected_populations: Children under 5, pregnant/lactating women, elderly, displaced populations

crisis_types.definition: Expulsion of lava, ash, and gases from a volcanic crater, causing destruction through lava flows, pyroclastic flows, lahars, and ashfall.
crisis_types.affected_populations: Communities within volcanic hazard zones, agricultural communities

crisis_types.definition: Downslope movement of rock, soil, and debris, often triggered by heavy rainfall, earthquakes, or volcanic activity.
crisis_types.affected_populations: Hillside communities, informal settlements on steep terrain

crisis_types.definition: Large-scale forced movement of populations due to conflict, violence, persecution, or natural disasters.
crisis_types.affected_populations: Refugees, internally displaced persons, stateless persons, asylum seekers

crisis_types.definition: Series of ocean waves caused by undersea earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, or landslides, capable of devastating coastal areas.
crisis_types.affected_populations: Coastal communities, fishing villages, low-lying island populations

crisis_types.definition: Humanitarian crisis involving multiple causal factors — typically conflict combined with natural disaster, food insecurity, and governance failure — requiring international response.
example_events: Democratic Republic of Congo (conflict + Ebola + displacement)
crisis_types.affected_populations: Multiple overlapping vulnerable groups across large geographical areas

crisis_types.definition: Major accident at industrial facility causing mass casualties, environmental contamination, or toxic exposure.
crisis_types.affected_populations: Workers, nearby residents, downwind/downstream communities

crisis_types.definition: Prolonged period of abnormally high temperatures exceeding local thresholds, causing heat-related illness and mortality.
crisis_types.affected_populations: Elderly, outdoor workers, urban poor, people with chronic illnesses

crisis_types.definition: Uncontrolled fire spreading through vegetation, exacerbated by drought, high temperatures, and wind.
crisis_types.affected_populations: Rural and peri-urban communities, wildlife, agricultural communities

crisis_types.definition: Situation where a significant portion of the population lacks adequate access to food, classified using the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC).
example_events: Global food crisis 2022 (345 million food insecure)
crisis_types.affected_populations: Children under 5, pregnant/lactating women, smallholder farmers, displaced populations

crisis_types.definition: Rapid cross-border movement of large numbers of people fleeing persecution, conflict, or violence, seeking international protection.
crisis_types.affected_populations: Refugees, unaccompanied minors, women and girls, persons with disabilities

crisis_types.definition: Release of radioactive materials from nuclear facility accidents, weapon detonation, or radiological dispersal devices.
crisis_types.affected_populations: Populations within fallout zone, first responders, agricultural communities

crisis_types.definition: Massive swarms of desert locusts devastating crops and pasture across wide areas, threatening food security of millions.
example_events: East Africa locust crisis 2020 (worst in 25 years)
crisis_types.affected_populations: Smallholder farmers, pastoralist communities, food-insecure populations

crisis_types.definition: Prolonged period of abnormally low temperatures causing hypothermia, frostbite, and excess mortality, particularly affecting displaced populations.
crisis_types.affected_populations: Displaced populations in tents/temporary shelter, homeless, elderly, young children

statistics.stat: 110 million forcibly displaced worldwide
statistics.context: Highest number ever recorded, including 36.4 million refugees, 62.5 million IDPs, and 6.1 million asylum seekers

statistics.stat: 339 million people need humanitarian assistance
statistics.context: A record high, up from 274 million in 2022

statistics.stat: 55.3 billion USD requested for humanitarian response
statistics.context: Only about 35% of humanitarian appeals are typically funded

statistics.stat: 45.7 million children under 5 suffer acute malnutrition
statistics.context: Of which 13.6 million are severely wasted, at immediate risk of death

statistics.stat: 2.2 billion people lack safely managed drinking water
statistics.context: Including 703 million without basic water service; 115 million drink untreated surface water

statistics.stat: 3.5 billion people lack safely managed sanitation
statistics.context: Including 419 million practicing open defecation

statistics.stat: Sphere minimum: 15 litres of water per person per day
statistics.context: Survival needs: 2.5-3L drinking, 2-6L cooking, 2-6L personal hygiene; 250 people per water point maximum

statistics.stat: Sphere minimum: 3.5 square metres of covered living space per person
statistics.context: In warm climates; cold climates may require more for heating efficiency. Excludes cooking space

statistics.stat: Sphere minimum: 2,100 kilocalories per person per day
statistics.context: Average population energy requirement; actual needs vary by age, sex, activity level, and climate

statistics.stat: Sphere minimum: 45 square metres per person in planned camp settings
statistics.context: Including infrastructure, roads, firebreaks; 30m² in emergency phase is acceptable

statistics.stat: 1 toilet per 20 people maximum in emergency phase
statistics.context: Separate facilities for men and women; maximum 50m from dwellings; with handwashing stations

statistics.stat: Crude mortality rate threshold: 1 death per 10,000 per day
statistics.context: Double the baseline indicates emergency; the Under-5 mortality emergency threshold is 2 per 10,000 per day

statistics.stat: Global Acute Malnutrition (GAM) emergency threshold: 15%
statistics.context: GAM 10-14% is serious; 15%+ is critical emergency requiring immediate therapeutic intervention

statistics.stat: 78% of refugees hosted by low- and middle-income countries
statistics.context: Top hosts: Turkey (3.6M), Iran (3.4M), Colombia (2.9M), Germany (2.6M), Pakistan (2.1M)

statistics.stat: 50% of refugees are women and girls
statistics.context: Women and girls face heightened risks of sexual and gender-based violence in displacement

statistics.stat: 40% of internally displaced are children
statistics.source: IDMC Global Report on Internal Displacement
statistics.context: Children disproportionately affected by displacement with disrupted education and protection risks

statistics.stat: 258 million children out of school worldwide
statistics.context: Crisis-affected children are 2.5 times more likely to be out of school

statistics.stat: 1 health facility per 10,000 population in emergencies
statistics.context: With referral hospital access for populations of 250,000; 50 consultations per clinician per day maximum

statistics.stat: 20 litres of water per person per day for health facilities
statistics.context: In addition to the 15L/person/day for domestic use; surgical facilities need more

statistics.stat: 274 million people needed humanitarian assistance in 2022
statistics.context: Up from 235 million in 2021, reflecting escalating crises and climate impacts

statistics.stat: Climate-related disasters displaced 32.6 million people in 2022
statistics.context: Weather-related events cause 3x more displacement than conflict; floods are the leading cause

statistics.stat: Over 60% of maternal deaths occur in humanitarian settings
statistics.context: Minimum Initial Service Package (MISP) for reproductive health must be implemented within first 48 hours

statistics.stat: 1 in 5 people in conflict-affected areas has a mental health condition
statistics.context: Prevalence of depression, anxiety, and PTSD significantly elevated in crisis-affected populations

statistics.stat: 68 cents of every dollar of humanitarian funding goes to food
statistics.source: Development Initiatives Global Humanitarian Assistance Report
statistics.context: Followed by multi-sector, health, and shelter/NFI; protection and education chronically underfunded

statistics.stat: Average length of displacement is 20+ years for refugees
statistics.context: Protracted displacement situations affect 78% of all refugees; most will never return home

statistics.stat: Over 4,000 aid workers attacked between 2003-2023
statistics.context: 2023 was the deadliest year on record with 280+ killed; 33 countries reported attacks

statistics.stat: Humanitarian coordination system has 11 clusters
statistics.context: WASH, Health, Nutrition, Education, Shelter/NFI, Protection, Food Security, Camp Coordination, Emergency Telecommunications, Logistics, Early Recovery

statistics.stat: Sphere standard: 1 community health worker per 1,000 population
statistics.context: For community-based surveillance and health promotion in emergency settings

statistics.stat: 20 people per latrine in emergency settings maximum
statistics.context: With separation by sex and lockable from inside; well-lit and within 50m of shelters

terminology.IDP: Internally Displaced Person — someone forced to flee their home but who has not crossed an international border. Unlike refugees, IDPs remain under the jurisdiction (and responsibility) of their own government.
terminology.UNHCR: United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees — the UN agency mandated to protect refugees, forcibly displaced communities, and stateless people. Lead agency for the Protection, Shelter/NFI, and Camp Coordination clusters.
terminology.OCHA: United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs — coordinates the global humanitarian response, manages the Central Emergency Response Fund (CERF), and produces the annual Global Humanitarian Overview.
terminology.WASH: Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene — one of the core sectors of humanitarian response. UNICEF leads the global WASH cluster. Sphere minimum standards include 15L/person/day water and 1 toilet per 20 people.
terminology.IPC: Integrated Food Security Phase Classification — a 5-phase scale for classifying food insecurity severity. Phase 1 (Minimal) to Phase 5 (Famine). Used by WFP, FAO, and governments to trigger response.
terminology.NFI: Non-Food Items — essential household items distributed in emergencies including blankets, cooking sets, hygiene kits, jerry cans, sleeping mats, and tarpaulins.
terminology.GBV: Gender-Based Violence — violence directed at a person based on their gender. Includes sexual violence, intimate partner violence, harmful traditional practices, and trafficking. Prevention and response is a cross-cutting concern in all humanitarian sectors.
terminology.CERF: Central Emergency Response Fund — OCHA-managed pooled fund that provides rapid initial funding for life-saving humanitarian action at the onset of emergencies. Provides up to $500M annually.
terminology.HRP: Humanitarian Response Plan — the annual strategic plan for a humanitarian operation, developed by the humanitarian country team under the Humanitarian Coordinator. Defines priorities, targets, and funding requirements.
terminology.CHS: Core Humanitarian Standard on Quality and Accountability — a set of 9 commitments that organizations and individuals involved in humanitarian response can use to improve quality and effectiveness.
terminology.Sphere Standards: A set of minimum standards in humanitarian response across four sectors (WASH, Food Security and Nutrition, Shelter and Settlement, Health) established by the Sphere Association. The Sphere Handbook 2018 is the current edition.
terminology.IASC: Inter-Agency Standing Committee — the highest-level humanitarian coordination forum, bringing together UN and non-UN organizations. Develops humanitarian policy, allocates responsibilities, and manages the cluster system.
terminology.cluster_system: The coordination mechanism established by the IASC Humanitarian Reform of 2005. Organizes humanitarian response into 11 thematic clusters, each led by a designated agency, to improve coordination and reduce gaps.
terminology.protection: Ensuring the safety, dignity, and rights of people affected by conflict and disaster. Encompasses child protection, GBV prevention, mine action, housing/land/property rights, and legal aid. UNHCR leads the global Protection cluster.
terminology.nexus: Humanitarian-Development-Peace Nexus — approach linking humanitarian action, development cooperation, and peace-building to reduce vulnerability and address root causes. Sometimes called 'triple nexus'.
terminology.do_no_harm: Fundamental humanitarian principle requiring that aid delivery does not inadvertently cause or exacerbate harm. Requires conflict sensitivity analysis, market impact assessment, and protection mainstreaming.
terminology.AAP: Accountability to Affected Populations — commitment to use power responsibly by taking account of, giving account to, and being held to account by the people affected by humanitarian action. CHS Commitment 4 and 5.
terminology.PSEA: Protection from Sexual Exploitation and Abuse — standards and mechanisms to prevent and respond to sexual exploitation and abuse by humanitarian workers. Zero-tolerance policy applies to all UN and partner staff.
terminology.cash_transfer_programming: Delivering assistance through cash or vouchers rather than in-kind goods. Includes unconditional cash transfers, conditional transfers, vouchers, and cash-for-work. Preferred when markets function.
terminology.needs_assessment: Systematic process of collecting and analyzing information to determine humanitarian needs, priorities, and response options. Types include initial rapid assessment, sector-specific assessment, and multi-sector needs assessment (MSNA).
terminology.PDNA: Post-Disaster Needs Assessment — joint government, UN, EU, World Bank methodology for assessing damage, losses, and recovery needs after a disaster. Covers physical damage, economic losses, and human impact.
terminology.DRR: Disaster Risk Reduction — systematic approach to identifying, assessing, and reducing disaster risks through prevention, mitigation, and preparedness. Guided by the Sendai Framework 2015-2030.
terminology.EWS: Early Warning System — integrated system for monitoring, forecasting, and communicating hazard information to enable timely protective action. Must be people-centered with clear dissemination channels.
terminology.humanitarian_access: The ability of humanitarian organizations to reach affected populations and for affected populations to access assistance and services. Requires negotiation with parties to conflict.
terminology.humanitarian_principles: Four core principles guiding humanitarian action: Humanity (alleviate suffering), Neutrality (not taking sides), Impartiality (based on need alone), Independence (autonomous from political objectives).
terminology.MISP: Minimum Initial Service Package for Reproductive Health — priority activities that must be implemented at the onset of every humanitarian crisis to prevent excess maternal and neonatal mortality and morbidity.
terminology.MHPSS: Mental Health and Psychosocial Support — any type of local or outside support that aims to protect or promote psychosocial well-being and prevent mental health conditions. Follows the IASC intervention pyramid.
terminology.SGBV: Sexual and Gender-Based Violence — broader term encompassing all forms of violence rooted in gender inequality, including sexual violence, domestic violence, forced marriage, and female genital mutilation.
terminology.PoC: Protection of Civilians — in peacekeeping contexts, the mandate to protect civilians from physical violence. In humanitarian contexts, broader protection activities including advocacy, monitoring, and response.
terminology.HNO: Humanitarian Needs Overview — the annual analysis of humanitarian needs that informs the Humanitarian Response Plan. Uses data from needs assessments, population estimates, and severity classifications.
terminology.INFORM: Index for Risk Management — a composite indicator that identifies countries at risk of humanitarian crisis and disaster. Combines hazard/exposure, vulnerability, and lack of coping capacity scores (0-10 scale).
terminology.SADD: Sex and Age Disaggregated Data — the collection and analysis of data broken down by sex and age groups. Essential for understanding differential impacts and ensuring equitable response.
terminology.GAM: Global Acute Malnutrition — combined prevalence of moderate and severe acute malnutrition in children 6-59 months. Emergency threshold: 15% or above. Measured by weight-for-height z-score or mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC).
terminology.SAM: Severe Acute Malnutrition — most dangerous form of malnutrition, identified by very low weight-for-height (below -3 z-scores), visible severe wasting, or MUAC below 115mm, or bilateral pitting oedema.
terminology.MAM: Moderate Acute Malnutrition — identified by weight-for-height between -3 and -2 z-scores, or MUAC between 115-124mm. Treated through supplementary feeding programs.
terminology.MUAC: Mid-Upper Arm Circumference — simple anthropometric measurement used for rapid nutrition screening. Below 115mm = SAM, 115-124mm = MAM, 125mm+ = acceptable. Used in community screening.
terminology.OTP: Outpatient Therapeutic Programme — community-based approach for treating SAM without medical complications using Ready-to-Use Therapeutic Food (RUTF). Treats 80%+ of SAM cases without hospitalization.
terminology.RUTF: Ready-to-Use Therapeutic Food — energy-dense, micronutrient-enriched paste (typically peanut-based) for treating severe acute malnutrition. Does not require water or cooking; long shelf life.
terminology.WFP: World Food Programme — the world's largest humanitarian organization addressing hunger. Lead agency for the Food Security and Logistics clusters. Reached 160 million people in 2022.
terminology.UNICEF: United Nations Children's Fund — UN agency responsible for providing humanitarian and developmental aid to children. Lead agency for WASH, Nutrition, and Education clusters.
terminology.WHO: World Health Organization — UN agency responsible for international public health. Lead agency for the Health cluster. Coordinates disease surveillance, outbreak response, and health system support.
terminology.ICRC: International Committee of the Red Cross — independent, neutral humanitarian organization with special mandate under International Humanitarian Law. Works in conflict zones; visits detainees; restores family links.
terminology.IFRC: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies — coordinates international disaster response and development programs of 192 National Societies. Manages disaster relief, health, and resilience programs.
terminology.MSF: Medecins Sans Frontieres (Doctors Without Borders) — international medical humanitarian organization that provides emergency medical aid. Known for independence from political influence and speaking out (temoignage).
terminology.HDX: Humanitarian Data Exchange — OCHA-managed open data platform for sharing humanitarian datasets. Hosts 20,000+ datasets from 250+ organizations across 260+ locations. Key source for humanitarian indicators.
terminology.ReliefWeb: OCHA information service providing 24/7 coverage of humanitarian crises. Publishes situation reports, maps, job listings, and training. The main source for up-to-date crisis information.
terminology.IHL: International Humanitarian Law — body of law (primarily the Geneva Conventions and their Additional Protocols) that regulates the conduct of armed conflict and protects those not participating in hostilities.
terminology.PoC_site: Protection of Civilians site — designated area within or adjacent to a UN peacekeeping base where displaced civilians receive physical protection. Distinct from refugee camps in legal status and management.
terminology.DTM: Displacement Tracking Matrix — IOM system for tracking and monitoring displacement and population mobility. Provides data on displacement figures, locations, needs, and vulnerabilities.
terminology.4W: Who does What, Where, and When — basic coordination tool mapping humanitarian activities by organization, sector, location, and timeframe to identify gaps and overlaps.
terminology.ConOps: Concept of Operations — plan describing how humanitarian operations will be conducted in a specific context, including access, logistics, security, and coordination arrangements.
terminology.INGO: International Non-Governmental Organization — non-profit organization operating across national borders for humanitarian or development purposes. Examples: Save the Children, Oxfam, World Vision, IRC.
terminology.LNGO: Local/National Non-Governmental Organization — civil society organization based in the affected country. Localization agenda promotes shifting more funding and decision-making power to LNGOs.
terminology.localization: Agenda to shift humanitarian leadership and resources to local and national actors. Grand Bargain commitment: 25% of funding to local organizations by 2020 (target not yet met).
terminology.Grand_Bargain: Agreement between major humanitarian donors and organizations to improve efficiency and effectiveness. Commitments include more cash programming, localization, reduced earmarking, and harmonized reporting.
terminology.flash_appeal: Rapid fundraising tool issued within days of a sudden-onset emergency, before a full Humanitarian Response Plan can be developed. Typically covers 3-6 months of immediate needs.
terminology.contingency_planning: Process of preparing for potential future events by analyzing risks, developing response strategies, and positioning resources. Required annually for all humanitarian country teams.
terminology.SPHERE_WASH_standard_1: Water supply: minimum 15 litres of water per person per day for drinking, cooking, and personal hygiene. Maximum 500 metres to nearest water point; queuing time no more than 30 minutes.
terminology.SPHERE_WASH_standard_2: Water quality: water must be palatable and of sufficient quality for drinking and cooking. Free from contamination at point of delivery. Residual chlorine 0.2-0.5 mg/l at point of delivery.
terminology.SPHERE_shelter_standard: Minimum 3.5 m² covered living space per person in warm climates. Shelter must provide protection from climate, ensure privacy and dignity, and be culturally appropriate.
terminology.SPHERE_food_standard: Minimum 2,100 kcal per person per day average energy intake. Adequate macronutrient and micronutrient composition. No more than 10% of total energy from sugar.
terminology.SPHERE_health_standard: Access to primary healthcare within one hour's walk. 1 health facility per 10,000 population. 50 outpatient consultations per clinician per day maximum. Essential drugs and supplies per WHO list.
terminology.early_recovery: Approach linking relief and development, starting early in the humanitarian response. Includes livelihoods, governance, infrastructure, and environmental restoration. UNDP leads the Early Recovery cluster.
terminology.humanitarian_corridor: Negotiated route allowing safe passage of humanitarian aid and/or civilian movement through areas of conflict. Requires agreement of all parties to the conflict.
terminology.camp_management: Organized coordination and administration of displacement sites, including service delivery, site planning, community governance, and eventual closure. IOM leads for natural disaster; UNHCR for conflict.
terminology.durable_solutions: Long-term resolution to displacement: voluntary repatriation (return), local integration (settle in host area), or resettlement (move to third country). Refugees have the right to choose.
terminology.refoulement: The forcible return of refugees or asylum seekers to a country where they face serious threats to life or freedom. Prohibited under the 1951 Refugee Convention (non-refoulement principle).
terminology.RSD: Refugee Status Determination — legal or administrative process for determining whether a person qualifies as a refugee. Conducted by states or UNHCR where states lack capacity.
terminology.CCCM: Camp Coordination and Camp Management — humanitarian cluster responsible for organized displacement site management. IOM leads for natural disasters, UNHCR leads for conflict displacement.
terminology.ETC: Emergency Telecommunications Cluster — provides shared telecommunications services (internet, radio) in humanitarian operations. Led by WFP. Enables coordination and safety communication.
terminology.logistics_cluster: Coordination platform for logistics in humanitarian operations, led by WFP. Manages common transport, storage, and supply chain services. Activated in large-scale emergencies.
terminology.standby_partners: Organizations that maintain trained staff and equipment on standby for rapid deployment to humanitarian emergencies. Examples: Norwegian Refugee Council (NORCAP), RedR, Danish Refugee Council.
terminology.UNDAC: United Nations Disaster Assessment and Coordination — rapidly deployable team of emergency management specialists from OCHA. Deploys within 12-48 hours of a sudden-onset disaster.
terminology.USAR: Urban Search and Rescue — specialized emergency response involving locating, extricating, and providing initial medical treatment to victims trapped in collapsed structures.
terminology.INSARAG: International Search and Rescue Advisory Group — UN network responsible for coordinating international USAR response. Classifies USAR teams as Light, Medium, or Heavy.
terminology.IHP: International Humanitarian Partnership — network of governmental emergency management agencies (civil protection) that provides capacity to support the humanitarian system.
terminology.PFA: Psychological First Aid — evidence-informed approach for assisting people in the immediate aftermath of disaster and terrorism, reducing initial distress and fostering short/long-term adaptive functioning.
terminology.SGBV_referral_pathway: Established system of services and support for GBV survivors including medical care, psychosocial support, legal assistance, safety/security, and socioeconomic reintegration.
terminology.feedback_mechanism: System allowing affected populations to provide feedback, complaints, and suggestions about humanitarian assistance. Required by AAP and CHS commitments.
terminology.multipurpose_cash: Unrestricted cash transfer to cover a household's basic needs across multiple sectors. Calculated based on Minimum Expenditure Basket (MEB) analysis.
terminology.MEB: Minimum Expenditure Basket — the basket of essential goods and services a household needs monthly, used to calculate cash transfer amounts. Includes food, rent, transport, health, education, communication.
terminology.EMMA: Emergency Market Mapping and Analysis — rapid market analysis tool used in humanitarian response to assess whether markets can support cash-based interventions.
terminology.PDM: Post-Distribution Monitoring — assessment conducted after aid distribution to verify receipt, measure satisfaction, identify challenges, and adjust programming accordingly.

workflows.description: First assessment within 72 hours of emergency onset to determine scale, severity, and immediate priorities.
steps: 1. Activate assessment team and review secondary data
2. Establish contact with local authorities and affected communities
3. Conduct rapid multi-sector observation and key informant interviews
4. Estimate affected population, displacement, and infrastructure damage
5. Identify immediate life-saving priorities and access constraints
6. Produce initial situation report within 24 hours
7. Brief humanitarian country team and activate clusters as needed

workflows.description: Annual planning process for humanitarian operations, led by the Humanitarian Coordinator.
steps: 1. Conduct Humanitarian Needs Overview (HNO) based on multi-sector needs assessment
2. Define strategic objectives aligned with identified needs
3. Clusters develop sector-specific response strategies
4. Determine target populations using vulnerability criteria
5. Calculate financial requirements per cluster and activity
6. Draft and peer-review the HRP document
7. Launch appeal and activate Financial Tracking Service

workflows.description: Establishing emergency shelter for displaced populations following Sphere standards.
steps: 1. Identify suitable sites (drainage, access, distance from hazards)
2. Plan layout: 45m²/person including infrastructure, minimum 30m² in emergency phase
3. Ensure 3.5m² covered living space per person minimum
4. Position WASH facilities within 50m of shelters
5. Establish firebreaks every 300m and access roads
6. Distribute NFI kits (blankets, mats, cooking sets, jerry cans)
7. Register population and establish community governance
8. Set up lighting in common areas for protection

workflows.description: Establishing emergency water supply meeting Sphere WASH standards.
steps: 1. Assess existing water sources and infrastructure damage
2. Establish minimum 15L per person per day (7.5L in survival phase)
3. Position water points within 500m of shelters, max 250 people per point
4. Test water quality: 0 fecal coliforms per 100ml at point of delivery
5. Ensure residual chlorine 0.2-0.5 mg/L at delivery point
6. Install water storage: minimum 2 vessels of 10-20L per household
7. Monitor queue times (max 30 minutes) and adjust distribution
8. Transition from water trucking to sustainable sources

workflows.description: Medical triage process for mass casualty incidents in humanitarian emergencies.
steps: 1. Establish triage point at safe distance from hazard
2. Apply START triage: walking wounded (GREEN), breathing after repositioning (RED), breathing spontaneously (YELLOW), not breathing after repositioning (BLACK)
3. Tag patients with triage categories
4. Establish treatment areas by priority
5. Coordinate evacuation to referral facilities (1 per 250,000 population)
6. Activate blood bank and surgical capacity
7. Document casualties and notify families through family tracing

workflows.description: Designing and implementing cash or voucher assistance programs.
steps: 1. Conduct market assessment (EMMA or similar) to verify market functionality
2. Calculate Minimum Expenditure Basket (MEB) for target area
3. Determine transfer value and frequency
4. Select delivery mechanism (mobile money, bank transfer, voucher)
5. Register beneficiaries with SADD and vulnerability criteria
6. Conduct baseline assessment
7. Distribute transfers and monitor through PDM
8. Adjust programming based on market monitoring and beneficiary feedback

workflows.description: Responding to acute malnutrition emergency (GAM above 15% threshold).
steps: 1. Conduct SMART nutrition survey to establish GAM/SAM prevalence
2. Activate CMAM protocol: OTP for uncomplicated SAM, SC for complicated SAM
3. Distribute RUTF (Ready-to-Use Therapeutic Food) through OTP sites
4. Establish supplementary feeding for MAM (MUAC 115-124mm)
5. Screen all children 6-59 months using MUAC at community level
6. Implement blanket supplementary feeding if GAM >15% with aggravating factors
7. Address underlying causes: WASH, food security, health services
8. Monitor recovery rates (target: >75% for SAM treatment)

workflows.description: Integrating protection principles across all humanitarian sectors.
steps: 1. Conduct protection risk analysis as part of needs assessment
2. Apply do-no-harm analysis to all program design
3. Ensure meaningful access for all groups (disability, age, gender)
4. Establish feedback and complaints mechanisms including for sensitive issues
5. Train all sector staff on protection principles and referral pathways
6. Disaggregate all data by sex and age (SADD)
7. Integrate GBV risk mitigation in shelter, WASH, and distribution design
8. Monitor protection incidents and adapt programming accordingly

workflows.description: Responding to disease outbreaks (cholera, measles, Ebola) in humanitarian settings.
steps: 1. Confirm outbreak through laboratory testing and case definitions
2. Activate surveillance: establish case definitions and reporting chain
3. Set up treatment facilities (CTCs for cholera, ETUs for Ebola)
4. Implement infection prevention and control (IPC) measures
5. Launch risk communication and community engagement (RCCE)
6. Conduct contact tracing (for diseases requiring it)
7. Implement vaccination campaign if vaccine available
8. Maintain safe and dignified burials if needed
9. Monitor transmission chains and declare end of outbreak

workflows.description: Re-establishing education services in crisis settings following INEE Minimum Standards.
steps: 1. Assess education needs: schools damaged, teachers displaced, children out of school
2. Establish temporary learning spaces within 72 hours where safe
3. Provide psychosocial support through structured activities
4. Recruit and train teachers (prioritize affected community members)
5. Distribute learning materials and school supplies
6. Ensure safe learning environment (protection from hazards, GBV, recruitment)
7. Coordinate with Education cluster on curriculum and certification
8. Plan transition to formal education and long-term recovery

workflows.description: Registration process for newly arrived refugees.
steps: 1. Establish reception center at border/entry point
2. Conduct level 1 registration (headcount, demographics, basic biometrics)
3. Screen for specific needs (medical, protection, family separation)
4. Provide emergency assistance (food, water, shelter, medical care)
5. Conduct individual registration with full biometric data (PRIMES/proGres)
6. Issue documentation (refugee certificate or attestation)
7. Refer cases requiring specific attention (unaccompanied minors, GBV survivors)
8. Conduct refugee status determination (RSD) if individual process required

workflows.description: Preparing and conducting humanitarian coordination meetings (cluster or inter-cluster).
steps: 1. Circulate agenda and key documents 48 hours in advance
2. Prepare 4W (Who, What, Where, When) matrix update
3. Compile gap analysis based on current response vs identified needs
4. Present new assessment findings or situation changes
5. Identify and discuss operational bottlenecks (access, funding, capacity)
6. Agree on action points with responsible focal points and deadlines
7. Distribute meeting minutes within 24 hours
8. Track action point completion at next meeting

decision_frameworks.name: IPC Phase Classification
decision_frameworks.description: Framework for classifying food insecurity severity, used to trigger humanitarian response.

phases.name: Minimal
phases.description: Households can meet essential food and non-food needs without engaging in atypical strategies

phases.name: Stressed
phases.description: Households have minimally adequate food but cannot afford essential non-food expenditures

phases.name: Crisis
phases.description: Households face food consumption gaps or are marginally able to meet minimum food needs through asset depletion or crisis strategies

phases.name: Emergency
phases.description: Households face large food consumption gaps, very high acute malnutrition, or excess mortality

phases.name: Famine
phases.description: At least 20% of households face extreme food gaps; GAM >30%; death rate >2/10,000/day

decision_frameworks.name: Humanitarian Programme Cycle
decision_frameworks.description: The coordinated series of actions for preparing and delivering humanitarian response.

phases.name: Needs Assessment and Analysis
phases.description: Multi-sector needs assessment, Humanitarian Needs Overview (HNO)

phases.name: Strategic Response Planning
phases.description: Humanitarian Response Plan (HRP) development with strategic objectives

phases.name: Resource Mobilization
phases.description: Appeals, flash appeals, CERF, country-based pooled funds

phases.name: Implementation and Monitoring
phases.description: Cluster-based response delivery with monitoring framework

phases.name: Operational Review and Evaluation
phases.description: Periodic monitoring reports, real-time evaluations, lessons learned

decision_frameworks.name: IASC Emergency Response Activation
decision_frameworks.description: System-wide activation levels for humanitarian emergencies.

phases.name: Level 1 (Country-level)
phases.description: Country team can manage with existing capacity; regional bureau oversight

phases.name: Level 2 (Regional)
phases.description: Significant crisis requiring augmented response; regional surge deployment

phases.name: Level 3 (System-wide)
phases.description: Major sudden-onset or rapidly deteriorating crisis; system-wide mobilization; ERC activates protocols; maximum surge; senior leadership deployment

decision_frameworks.name: Market Functionality Assessment
decision_frameworks.description: Decision framework for determining cash-based intervention feasibility.

criteria.question: Are essential goods available in sufficient quantity?
Can affected populations physically and safely reach markets?
Are prices stable or predictably trending?
Can vendors scale up supply to meet increased demand?
Are transfer mechanisms (mobile money, banks) functional?
Does cash create protection risks (theft, diversion, exploitation)?

decision_frameworks.name: Severity Classification (OCHA)
decision_frameworks.description: 5-level severity scale used in Humanitarian Needs Overviews.

phases.name: Minimal
phases.description: Living standards are acceptable; coping mechanisms not depleted

phases.name: Stress
phases.description: Living standards are below acceptable; coping mechanisms beginning to deplete

phases.name: Severe
phases.description: Living standards significantly below acceptable; reliance on negative coping

phases.name: Extreme
phases.description: Collapse of living standards; irreversible coping; excess mortality likely

phases.name: Catastrophic
phases.description: Total collapse of living standards; mass mortality if no immediate intervention

decision_frameworks.name: Sendai Framework Priorities
decision_frameworks.description: Four priority areas for disaster risk reduction 2015-2030.

priorities.name: Understanding disaster risk
priorities.description: Risk assessments, data collection, early warning systems

priorities.name: Strengthening disaster risk governance
priorities.description: National and local DRR strategies, institutional frameworks

priorities.name: Investing in DRR for resilience
priorities.description: Structural and non-structural measures, social protection, financial instruments

priorities.name: Enhancing preparedness
priorities.description: Build back better, forecast-based action, contingency planning

decision_frameworks.name: CMAM Decision Tree
decision_frameworks.description: Community-based Management of Acute Malnutrition treatment protocol.

criteria.condition: MUAC < 115mm or bilateral oedema with complications
MUAC < 115mm or bilateral oedema without complications

decision_frameworks.name: Protection Risk Framework
decision_frameworks.description: Framework for assessing and prioritizing protection risks in humanitarian settings.

risk_categories.examples: Armed attacks on civilians, sexual violence, recruitment of children, landmines/ERW
Forced displacement, forced recruitment, extortion, restriction of movement
Denial of access to services, destruction of property, confiscation of documents
Exclusion from assistance, denial of rights, marginalization of groups

best_practices.rationale: Single-sector assessments miss interconnected needs. MSNA captures how food insecurity compounds health risks and how displacement affects education.

best_practices.practice: Default to cash when markets function
best_practices.rationale: Cash preserves dignity and choice, supports local markets, reduces logistics costs by 25-30%, and allows beneficiaries to prioritize their own needs.

best_practices.practice: Establish multiple feedback channels including anonymous options
best_practices.rationale: Single-channel feedback excludes populations with literacy, language, or access barriers. Sensitive complaints (PSEA, fraud) require confidential channels.

best_practices.practice: Apply data minimization and purpose limitation to all beneficiary data
best_practices.rationale: Over-collection of personal data in humanitarian settings creates protection risks. Collect only what is needed for the stated purpose; delete when no longer needed.
best_practices.reference: IASC Operational Guidance on Data Responsibility

best_practices.practice: Partner with and fund local organizations as lead implementers
best_practices.rationale: Local organizations have community trust, cultural knowledge, and sustained presence. Direct funding improves speed and sustainability of response.

best_practices.practice: Conduct gender analysis at the start of every response
best_practices.rationale: Crises affect men, women, boys, and girls differently. Without gender analysis, responses default to male-norm assumptions, excluding women from decision-making and missing specific vulnerabilities.

best_practices.practice: Apply the Washington Group Short Set for disability identification
best_practices.rationale: 15% of the global population has a disability. Crisis-affected persons with disabilities are disproportionately excluded from humanitarian services.
best_practices.reference: IASC Guidelines on Inclusion of Persons with Disabilities

best_practices.practice: Conduct environmental screening for all camp and program design
best_practices.rationale: Large-scale humanitarian operations can cause deforestation, water table depletion, and waste accumulation. Environmental damage undermines long-term recovery.

best_practices.practice: Design exit criteria from the start of any program
best_practices.rationale: Programs without exit strategies create dependency and are difficult to phase out. Define handover criteria, build local capacity, and transition to development actors.

best_practices.practice: Apply do-no-harm analysis to resource distribution
best_practices.rationale: Aid distribution can exacerbate tensions between groups, create incentives for conflict, or reinforce power imbalances. Analyze distributional effects before delivery.
best_practices.reference: CDA Collaborative Learning Projects — Do No Harm Framework

best_practices.rationale: Without operational mapping, clusters cannot identify gaps, duplications, or underserved areas. 4W matrices are the minimum viable coordination tool.

best_practices.practice: Use standardized data formats (IATI, P-codes, SADD)
best_practices.rationale: Non-standard data cannot be aggregated across organizations, making needs analysis and gap identification impossible at the coordination level.

best_practices.practice: Integrate protection across all sectors, not just protection-specific activities
best_practices.rationale: Protection risks arise in every sector: unsafe water points, lack of lighting in camps, registration processes that exclude vulnerable groups. All sector staff must consider protection.

best_practices.practice: Follow the IASC MHPSS intervention pyramid
best_practices.rationale: Most crisis-affected people need basic support and community-level interventions, not clinical services. Over-clinicalization wastes resources and can pathologize normal distress responses.
best_practices.reference: IASC Guidelines on Mental Health and Psychosocial Support

best_practices.practice: Pre-position emergency stocks within 72-hour reach of high-risk areas
best_practices.rationale: Response speed saves lives. Pre-positioned stocks eliminate procurement and shipping delays. UNHCR, UNICEF, WFP, and IFRC maintain global stockpiles.

case_studies.title: Syria Crisis Response 2011-present
case_studies.context: The largest displacement crisis of the 21st century, with 6.8 million refugees and 6.9 million internally displaced.
key_facts: Over 14 million people need humanitarian assistance inside Syria
Cross-border aid delivery mechanism authorized by UN Security Council Resolution 2165
Whole-of-Syria approach coordinates across government and opposition areas
Education disrupted for 2.4 million children
lessons_learned: Protracted crises require development approaches alongside humanitarian response
Cross-border mechanisms are essential when government consent is restricted
Early investment in cash programming proved more effective than in-kind aid

case_studies.title: Ebola Response West Africa 2014-2016
case_studies.context: Unprecedented Ebola outbreak in Guinea, Liberia, and Sierra Leone killing 11,325 people.
key_facts: 28,616 confirmed, probable, and suspected cases
Initial WHO response criticized as too slow
UNMEER — first-ever UN emergency health mission — established September 2014
Community engagement ultimately more effective than top-down measures
lessons_learned: Community trust is essential for outbreak response
Vertical health responses must be integrated with health system strengthening
Cultural practices (burial rituals) must be addressed respectfully, not overridden
International coordination mechanisms need faster activation triggers

case_studies.title: Nepal Earthquake Response 2015
case_studies.context: 7.8 magnitude earthquake killing 8,900 people and destroying 600,000 homes.
key_facts: 8 million people affected (nearly one-third of Nepal's population)
Over 500,000 houses destroyed, 250,000 damaged
International response mobilized within 24 hours
UNDAC team deployed within 12 hours
lessons_learned: Pre-positioned stocks enabled faster response than procurement
Coordination challenges with 450+ organizations responding
Cash programming more effective than material distribution in functioning markets
Build back better principles essential for seismic zones

case_studies.title: Rohingya Refugee Crisis 2017
case_studies.context: Mass displacement of 740,000 Rohingya from Myanmar to Bangladesh in weeks.
key_facts: Fastest-growing refugee crisis in 2017
Cox's Bazar became world's largest refugee camp (900,000 people)
Major monsoon and cyclone risks to camp population
Statelessness complicates durable solutions
lessons_learned: Mega-camps create protection and environmental challenges
Decentralized settlement preferable when land available
Registration and documentation essential from day one
Host community support prevents social tensions

case_studies.title: COVID-19 Humanitarian Impact 2020-2023
case_studies.context: Global pandemic compounding existing humanitarian crises and creating new vulnerabilities.
key_facts: Humanitarian needs increased by 40% in 2020
Supply chain disruptions affected food and medical supplies
Lockdowns prevented humanitarian access in many contexts
Accelerated adoption of remote programming and cash transfers
lessons_learned: Digital readiness is essential for humanitarian operations
Remote monitoring and verification methods needed development
Cash and voucher assistance proved more adaptable than in-kind
Pandemic preparedness must be integrated into humanitarian planning

case_studies.title: Pakistan Floods 2022
case_studies.context: Catastrophic monsoon flooding affecting 33 million people and submerging one-third of the country.
key_facts: 1,739 deaths; 33 million people affected
Estimated $30 billion in damages and economic losses
One-third of Pakistan's land area submerged
7.9 million people displaced; 2 million homes destroyed
lessons_learned: Climate change is amplifying disaster severity beyond historical patterns
Loss and damage funding mechanisms urgently needed
Early warning systems saved lives where they existed
Recovery requires years and development-scale funding

case_studies.title: Ukraine Crisis Response 2022-present
case_studies.context: Full-scale invasion displacing millions internally and across borders within weeks.
key_facts: 8 million internally displaced; 6.2 million refugees across Europe
Fastest and largest displacement crisis in Europe since WWII
Multipurpose cash assistance scaled rapidly using existing banking infrastructure
Integration approach in host countries rather than camp-based response
lessons_learned: Middle-income crisis contexts require different approaches than traditional humanitarian settings
Pre-existing infrastructure enables rapid cash-based response
Host country integration more viable than encampment in European context
Long-range weapons create new challenges for humanitarian access and protection

case_studies.title: Horn of Africa Drought 2022-2023
case_studies.context: Five consecutive failed rainy seasons creating worst drought in 40 years across Somalia, Ethiopia, and Kenya.
key_facts: Over 36 million people affected across the region
Somalia declared famine in parts of Bay region (IPC Phase 5)
7.8 million livestock deaths devastating pastoralist livelihoods
Anticipatory action and early response helped prevent worst outcomes
lessons_learned: Forecast-based action and early funding can prevent famine
Pastoral livelihoods need specific support (livestock insurance, destocking)
Multi-year drought requires sustained rather than surge response
Climate adaptation must be integrated with humanitarian response

water_supply.minimum: 15 litres per person per day for drinking, cooking, and personal hygiene
indicators: Maximum distance to water point: 500 metres
Minimum flow rate: 0.125 litres per second per tap
Survival allocation: 7.5 litres per person per day (first days only)

water_quality.minimum: Water is palatable and of sufficient quality for drinking and cooking without health risk
indicators: 0 faecal coliforms per 100ml at point of delivery
Residual chlorine 0.2-0.5 mg/L at point of delivery (turbidity <5 NTU)
Residual chlorine 0.5-1.0 mg/L when turbidity higher or disease risk
Turbidity below 5 NTU at point of delivery
No negative health effects from chemical or radiological contamination
Maximum 20 people per toilet (1 toilet per 20 people)
Separate facilities for men and women
Handwashing station with soap/ash at each toilet block
Well-lit or provision of torches for night use

hygiene.minimum: Access to hygiene items and understanding of key hygiene practices
indicators: Two water collection containers (10-20L) per household
Sufficient menstrual hygiene materials for women and girls

food_security.standard: Food Security Standard 1: General food security
food_security.minimum: 2,100 kilocalories per person per day (average population requirement)
indicators: Adequate micronutrient intake through fortified foods or supplements
No more than 10% of total energy from sugar

infant_feeding.standard: Food Security Standard 2: Infant and young child feeding
infant_feeding.minimum: Protection and support of breastfeeding; appropriate complementary feeding from 6 months
indicators: No distribution of breastmilk substitutes without meeting strict criteria
Code-compliant procurement and use of any necessary BMS

malnutrition_management.standard: Nutrition Standard: Management of acute malnutrition
malnutrition_management.minimum: Access to treatment for acute malnutrition
indicators: CMAM programme targets: >75% cure rate for SAM treatment
Average length of stay in OTP: 6-8 weeks

shelter_settlement.minimum: 3.5 square metres of covered living space per person in warm climates
indicators: 45 square metres per person in planned camps (including infrastructure)
30 square metres per person acceptable in emergency phase
Protection from climate (wind, rain, sun, cold)
Fire safety: 2 metres between structures minimum; 30m firebreaks every 300m
50 outpatient consultations per clinician per day maximum
Essential drugs available per WHO essential medicines list

communicable_disease.minimum: Surveillance system for epidemic-prone diseases established
indicators: Measles vaccination coverage >95% for children 6 months to 15 years
Case fatality rate for cholera treatment: <1%
Standard case definitions in use for all reportable diseases
Outbreak investigation within 48 hours of alert
Crude mortality rate baseline: 0.5 per 10,000 per day (sub-Saharan Africa: 0.8)
Emergency threshold: double the baseline CMR
Under-5 mortality rate emergency threshold: 2 per 10,000 per day
Neonatal mortality rate: tracked separately in MISP implementation
